nodes.name: k-colouring
nodes.statement: A {\em $k$-colouring} of a graph~$G=(V,E)$ is a mapping $c:V\to \{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$.

nodes.name: Colouring
nodes.statement: The {\sc Colouring} problem that of deciding whether a given graph~$G$ has a $k$-colouring for a given integer~$k$.
also_stated_at: The {\sc Colouring} problem asks whether the vertices of a graph can be coloured with at most~$k$ colours for a given integer~$k$ in such a way that no two adjacent vertices receive the same colour.

nodes.name: k-Colouring
nodes.statement: If~$k$ is fixed, then we write $k$-{\sc Colouring} instead.

nodes.name: NP-completeness of 3-Colouring
nodes.statement: It is well known that even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete~\cite{Lo73}.
conclusions: {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete

nodes.name: hereditary graph class
nodes.statement: A class is hereditary if it closed under vertex deletion.

nodes.name: Colouring perfect graphs in polynomial time (Grötschel-Lovász-Schrijver)
nodes.statement: A classical result in the area is due to Gr\"otschel, Lov\'asz, and Schrijver~\cite{GLS84}, who showed that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs

nodes.name: Hereditary classes are exactly H-free classes
nodes.statement: It is readily seen that a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free.
conclusions: a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free
equivalent_conditions: a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary
there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the minimal forbidden set
nodes.statement: If the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs, then~${\cal H}$ is unique.
assumptions: the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs
conclusions: ${\cal H}$ is unique

nodes.name: Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
nodes.statement: For example, the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes~\cite{CRST06}.
conclusions: the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes

nodes.name: Classification of Colouring on H-free graphs (Kral' et al.)
nodes.statement:
Kr\'al', Kratochv\'{\i}l, Tuza, and Woeginger~\cite{KKTW01} classified the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for the case where~${\cal H}$ consists of a single graph~$H$.
They proved that {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable if~$H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$ and {\sf NP}-complete otherwise.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable if~$H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$ and {\sf NP}-complete otherwise
nodes.statement_short: Colouring on $H$-free graphs is polynomial iff $H$ is an induced subgraph of $P_4$ or $P_1+P_3$, else NP-complete.

nodes.name: bigenic graph class
nodes.statement:
Kr\'al' et al.~\cite{KKTW01} also initiated a complexity study of {\sc Colouring} for graph classes defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$.
Such graph classes are said to be {\em bigenic}.
differentia: defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$

nodes.name: Open cases with two forbidden graphs on at most four vertices
nodes.statement:
For instance, if we forbid two graphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ with $|V(H_1)|\leq 4$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 4$, then there are three open cases left, namely when 
$(H_1,H_2)\in \{(K_{1,3},4P_1),\allowbreak (K_{1,3},2P_1+\nobreak P_2),\allowbreak (C_4,4P_1)\}$ (see~\cite{LM15} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fourvertices}).

nodes.name: Open cases with two connected forbidden graphs on at most five vertices
nodes.statement:
If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ are connected with $|V(H_1)|\leq 5$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 5$, then
there are four open cases left, namely when $H_1=P_5$ and $H_2\in \{\overline{C_3+2P_1},\overline{C_3+P_2},\overline{P_1+2P_2}\}$ (see~\cite{KMP} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}) and when $H_1=K_{1,3}$ and $H_2=\overline{C_4+P_1}$ (see~\cite{ML17} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}).

nodes.name: Precolouring Extension
nodes.statement:
For the first problem, we are given a graph~$G$, an integer~$k$ and a $k$-colouring~$c'$ defined on an induced subgraph of~$G$.
The question is whether~$G$ has a $k$-colouring~$c$ extending~$c'$.
nodes.statement_short: Given $G$, $k$ and a $k$-colouring of an induced subgraph, decide whether it extends to a $k$-colouring of $G$.

nodes.name: List Colouring
nodes.statement:
For the second problem, each vertex~$u$ of the input graph~$G$ has a list~$L(u)$ of colours.
Here the question is whether~$G$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$, that is, with $c(u)\in L(u)$ for all $u\in V(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether $G$ has a colouring with $c(u)\in L(u)$ for every vertex $u$.

nodes.name: almost classified graph
nodes.statement: We say that a connected graph~$H_1$ is {\em almost classified} if {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or {\sf NP}-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$.
differentia: {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or {\sf NP}-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$
also_stated_at: A connected graph~$H_1$ is almost classified if {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be polynomial-time solvable or {\sf NP}-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$.

nodes.name: Which connected graphs are almost classified?
Finite simple undirected graphs
nodes.statement: We consider only finite, undirected graphs without multiple edges or self-loops.

nodes.name: complement of a graph
nodes.statement:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph.
The {\em complement}~$\overline{G}$ of~$G$ is the graph with vertex set~$V(G)$ and an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$.
differentia: an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$

nodes.name: induced subgraph
nodes.statement: For a subset $S\subseteq V$, we let~$G[S]$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ {\em induced} by~$S$, which has vertex set~$S$ and edge set $\{uv\; |\; u,v\in S, uv\in E\}$.

nodes.name: (H_1,...,H_p)-free graph
nodes.statement:
Let $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$ be a set of graphs.
A graph~$G$ is {\em $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free} if~$G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$.
differentia: has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$
also_stated_at: Graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in a set~${\cal H}$ are said to be {\em ${\cal H}$-free}.
A graph is $(H_1,H_2)$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to~$H_1$ or~$H_2$.

nodes.name: H-free notation
nodes.statement: If~$p=1$, we may write $H_1$-free instead of $(H_1)$-free.

nodes.name: disjoint union
nodes.statement: The {\em disjoint union} $G+\nobreak H$ of two vertex-disjoint graphs~$G$ and~$H$ is the graph $(V(G)\cup V(H), E(G)\cup E(H))$.

nodes.name: rG (disjoint copies)
nodes.statement: The disjoint union of~$r$ copies of a graph~$G$ is denoted by~$rG$.

nodes.name: linear forest
nodes.statement: A {\em linear forest} is the disjoint union of one or more paths.

nodes.name: cycle, complete graph and path C_r, K_r, P_r
nodes.statement: The graphs~$C_r$, $K_r$ and~$P_r$ denote the cycle, complete graph and path on~$r$ vertices, respectively.

nodes.name: triangle
nodes.statement: The graph~$K_3$ is also known as the {\em triangle}.

nodes.name: complete bipartite graph K_{r,s}
nodes.statement: The graph~$K_{r,s}$ denotes the complete bipartite graph with partition classes of size~$r$ and~$s$, respectively.

nodes.name: claw
nodes.statement: The graph~$K_{1,3}$ is also called the {\em claw}.

nodes.name: subdivided claw S_{h,i,j}
nodes.statement: The graph~$S_{h,i,j}$, for $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$, denotes the {\em subdivided claw}, that is, the tree that has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$ and exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively.
differentia: has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$ and exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively

nodes.name: fork (chair)
nodes.statement: The graph~$S_{1,1,2}$ is also known as the {\em fork} or the {\em chair}.

nodes.name: T_{h,i,j} graph
nodes.statement:
The graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ with $0\leq h\leq i\leq j$ denotes the graph with vertices $a_0,\ldots,a_h$, $b_0,\ldots,b_i$ and $c_0,\ldots,c_j$ and edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_pa_{p+1}$ for $p \in \{0,\ldots, h-
obreak1\}$, $b_pb_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,i-
obreak 1\}$ and $c_pc_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,j-
obreak 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_{h,i,j}$: a triangle $a_0b_0c_0$ with pendant paths of lengths $h$, $i$, $j$ attached at its three vertices.

nodes.name: paw, bull, net, hammer
nodes.statement: The graph $T_{0,0,1}=\overline{P_1+P_3}$ is known as the {\em paw}, the graph~$T_{0,1,1}$ as the {\em bull}, the graph~$T_{1,1,1}$ as the {\em net}, and the graph~$T_{0,0,2}$ is known as the {\em hammer}; see also \figurename~\ref{fig:Thij-examples}.

nodes.name: T_{h,i,j} is a line graph of a subdivided claw
nodes.statement: Also note that~$T_{h,i,j}$ is the line graph of~$S_{h+1,i+1,j+1}$.
conclusions: $T_{h,i,j}$ is the line graph of~$S_{h+1,i+1,j+1}$

nodes.name: class T
nodes.statement: Let~${\cal T}$ be the class of graphs every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$.
differentia: every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$

nodes.name: Schindl's Theorem
nodes.statement: For $p\geq 1$, let $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$. Then {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs.
assumptions: $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs
nodes.label: t-schindl

nodes.name: Corollary 1 follows from Theorem 2
nodes.statement: In this section we prove the following result, from which it immediately follows that every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$ is almost classified.
nodes.statement_short: The corollary follows immediately from the finiteness theorem for pairs avoiding $K_{1,3}$ and $P_5$.

nodes.name: Finitely many open pairs avoiding the claw and P5
nodes.statement: There are only finitely many pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$, such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown.
conclusions: There are only finitely many pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$, such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown
also_stated_at: In fact we show that the number of pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs for which the complexity of {\sc Colouring} is unknown is finite if neither~$H_1$ nor~$H_2$ is isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$.
nodes.statement_short: Only finitely many connected pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ avoiding $K_{1,3}$ and $P_5$ have unknown Colouring complexity.
nodes.label: t-almost1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices. \medskip 
oindent Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases. \medskip 
oindent { f Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\ Then~$H_1$ is a path. First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+
obreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+
obreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs. Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant. \medskip 
oindent { f Case 2.} $H_1$ is a tree and not $K_{1,3}$-free, and~$H_2$ is $K_{1,3}$-free and not a tree.\ Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices. By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for the class of $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether $H_1$ is a path or a tree with a degree-3 vertex, using known NP-completeness results. Ramsey's Theorem then bounds $|V(H_2)|$ in every remaining case.

nodes.name: Observation on trees avoiding K_{1,3}, P_5 and induced subgraphs of P_4
nodes.statement:
We first make a useful observation.
Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$.
If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$.
If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$.
If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices.
We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\\
Then~$H_1$ is a path.
First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices.
It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}.

Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices.
By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices.
It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}.

Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant.
We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.

nodes.name: Golovach-Heggernes construction of (G_1,L)
nodes.statement:
Let $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only.
We construct an instance $(G_1,L)$ of {\sc List Colouring} as follows.
For each~$x_i$ we introduce a vertex, which we also denote by~$x_i$ and which we say is of {\em $x$-type}.
We define $L(x_1)=\{1,2\}$, $L(x_2)=\{3,4\},\ldots,L(x_n)=\{2n-1,2n\}$.
In this way, each~$x_i$ has one odd colour and one even colour in its list, and all lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint.
For each~$C_j$ we introduce two vertices, which we denote by~$C_j$ and~$C_j'$ and which we say are of {\em $C$-type}.
If $C_j=\{x_g,x_h,x_i\}$ with $L(x_g)=\{a,a+\nobreak 1\}$, $L(x_h)=\{b,b+\nobreak 1\}$ and $L(x_i)=\{c,c+\nobreak 1\}$, then we set $L(C_j)=\{a,b,c\}$ and $L(C_j')=\{a+\nobreak 1,b+\nobreak 1,c+\nobreak 1\}$.
Hence each~$C_j$ has only odd colours in its list and each~$C_j'$ has only even colours in its list.
To obtain the graph~$G_1$ we add an edge between every vertex of $x$-type and every vertex of $C$-type.
Note that~$G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$.
input: $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement:
We will prove that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $(C_4,3P_2,T_{0,2,2})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_1'}$, the set of $x$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_1'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex. \medskip 
oindent { f $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$; say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_1'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of $x$-type vertices and the set of $C$-type vertices each from a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, but~$u_2$ is non-adjacent to~$u_4$, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_2$ is of $x$-type and~$u_4$ is of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_1'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $C_4$-free. \medskip 
oindent { f $\mathbf{3P_2}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$3P_2$. As the $C$-type vertices and $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, one edge of~$H$ must consist of two $k$-type vertices. Therefore, if $\overline{H} \notin {\cal T}$, then {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs by Theorem~\ref{t-schindl}.
We may therefore assume that $\overline{H} \in {\cal T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Schindl's theorem to restrict to $\overline{H}\in{\cal T}$

nodes.name: $\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $T_{1,1,3}+P_{2n-1}
nodes.statement:
Since~$\overline{H}$ is $2C_3$-free, $\overline{H}$ can contain at most one component that is not a path.
Since~$\overline{H}$ is $(T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free, if~$\overline{H}$ does have a component that is not a path, then this component must be an induced subgraph of~$T_{1,1,3}$.
The union of components of~$\overline{H}$ that are isomorphic to paths form an induced subgraph of~$P_{2n-1}$.
Therefore~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $T_{1,1,3}+\nobreak P_{2n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $T_{1,1,3}+P_{2n-1}$

nodes.name: Part (ii): collect known polynomial-time cases
nodes.statement:
It is known that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(P_5,H)$-free graphs if~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of
$2P_1+\nobreak P_3$~\cite{Ma},
$P_1+\nobreak P_4$ (this follows from the fact that $(P_5,\overline{P_1+P_4})$-free graphs have clique-width at most~$5$~\cite{BLM04}; see also~\cite{BBKRS05} for a linear-time algorithm),
$P_2+\nobreak P_3$~\cite{ML17},
$P_5$~\cite{HL},
$T_{0,0,1}+\nobreak P_1$~\cite{KMP},
$T_{0,1,1}$~\cite{KMP},
$T_{0,0,2}$~\cite{KMP}
or $sP_1+\nobreak P_2$ for some integer $s\geq 0$~\cite{ML17}.\qed
